value.overview: The Lesser Goldfinch (Spinus psaltria) is a small, active finch of the Americas. It is recognizable by its short, conical bill, pointed wings, white wing patches, and black tail with white corners. Males vary geographically, from green-backed birds in western populations to black-backed birds farther east and south. The species commonly travels in flocks and feeds in open, disturbed, and partly wooded habitats. In Costa Rica, it is a locally familiar finch, especially in suitable highland and suburban areas.
value.classification: The Lesser Goldfinch belongs to the finch family Fringillidae and the genus Spinus. It is closely related to other goldfinches and siskins.
value.identification: This is a small finch with a relatively short, sharply pointed bill and a notched black tail marked with white corners. Adult males have bright yellow underparts, black wings, and either a green or black back depending on geographic population. Females and immature birds are duller, with olive or grayish upperparts, yellowish underparts, dark wings, and pale wing markings. In Costa Rica, males are generally the darker-backed southern form. Its rapid, varied song and frequent flocking behavior are also useful clues.
value.rangeHabitat: The Lesser Goldfinch ranges from the western and southwestern United States through Mexico and Central America, extending south into parts of northern South America. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly in the Central Valley and other suitable interior highlands, where it uses open woodland, forest edges, scrub, gardens, agricultural land, parks, and towns. It is less associated with dense, closed forest than with sunny habitats containing scattered trees, shrubs, weeds, and available seed-producing plants.
value.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the Lesser Goldfinch is generally treated as a resident species, although local or seasonal movements may occur. Birds from northern populations are migratory, while many populations farther south remain year-round. Costa Rican records also include occasional seasonal or irregular movements, but the species is not considered a regular long-distance migrant there.
value.breeding: Lesser Goldfinches usually breed in trees or shrubs, often near open areas, streams, gardens, or human habitation. The female builds a small cup nest from fine plant material and lines it with softer fibers. She generally lays several pale eggs and incubates them, while the male commonly helps feed her and later the young. Nesting in Costa Rica is possible and has been reported in the species' resident range, although detailed national breeding information is limited.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small seeds from grasses, weeds, herbs, shrubs, and trees. The birds also eat buds, plant material, and some small insects, especially when feeding nestlings. Lesser Goldfinches forage actively in treetops, brush, weedy fields, forest edges, farms, and gardens. They often hang upside down while extracting seeds and readily visit bird feeders offering sunflower or other small seeds.
value.behavior: Lesser Goldfinches are social and commonly form flocks, sometimes joining other seed-eating finches. They move quickly through vegetation and give soft calls while traveling or feeding. Outside the breeding period, groups may gather at reliable food and water sources. The species is adaptable and often uses suburban landscapes, parks, and gardens. Males may sing from exposed perches during the breeding season, but the birds are generally more conspicuous when feeding in groups.

conservation.populationTrend: No major global population decline is recognized, although abundance varies among regions and local populations may be affected by habitat change.
